title: Local Habitat Hunt
strapline: Out of the door with magnifiers and picture cards — the animals that live right here, on our patch.
intent: Children observe real animals in their own immediate environment, not only in books.
Looking closely and patiently is a scientific habit that has to be practised.
Children learn to handle living creatures gently and to return them where they were found.
The local patch becomes somewhere children know as learners, not just walk through.
Finding something alive prompts genuine questions that deserve genuine answers.
implementation: Go outside to look for birds, insects or worms — the garden, a wall, under a log.
Provide magnifying glasses, bug pots and picture cards for identifying what is found.
Teach the handling rules before you go: soft hands, look do not squash, always put it back.
Model using the magnifier properly rather than assuming children know how.
Extend the vocabulary in the moment: nest, burrow, shell, wing, antenna.
Let children lead where to look; they notice things adults walk past.
Record finds on a simple tally or map so the hunt builds over the half-term.
key_questions: Where do you think something might be hiding?
How many legs has it got? Can you count them?
How should we hold it so we keep it safe?
Why do you think it lives under there?
What did we find today that we did not find last time?

impact.text: Children build observation skills and awareness of living things.
Children treat living things gently as a matter of course.
Children know their local patch as a learner, not just a passer-by.
Children ask real questions about what they find and expect real answers.
Children count small groups — legs, spots, creatures — with growing accuracy.
Children take up specific new vocabulary and use it back to you.

enhancements: A bug hotel or log pile built by the children to make more homes to check.
A photographic record of every creature found, displayed as a class field guide.
A seasonal repeat of the same hunt to compare what is about in each term.
A magnifying station indoors with the treasures collected on the walk.
A worm investigation in a clear wormery so tunnelling can be watched over weeks.
A map of the garden marked with where each creature was found.

playing_exploring: Children choose where to search and follow their own curiosity.
Every hunt is genuinely open — nobody knows what will be found.
active_learning: Children look patiently and carefully, which takes real sustained attention.
They come back to a promising spot again and again.
creating_thinking: Children predict where a creature will be hiding, and test it.
They reason about why an animal lives in a particular place.
